content: Mortality and morbidity rates associated with neonatal sepsis and necrotising enterocolitis (NEC) remain significantly high, even with the use of potent antimicrobial agents. Agents that modulate inflammation, such as pentoxifylline (PTX), a phosphodiesterase inhibitor, may offer potential benefits in improving clinical outcomes. This review, which was initially published in 2003 and subsequently updated in 2011 and 2015, aims to evaluate the effectiveness and safety of intravenous PTX as an adjunct to antibiotic therapy in neonates with suspected or confirmed sepsis and those with NEC. The objective of this review was to determine whether PTX, when used alongside antibiotics, reduces mortality and morbidity in neonates with sepsis or NEC. The search strategy included databases such as CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, CINAHL, and trial registries, with the most recent search conducted in July 2022. Additionally, reference lists of identified clinical trials and conference abstracts were manually reviewed. The inclusion criteria focused on randomised controlled trials (RCTs) or quasi-RCTs that assessed the efficacy of PTX in combination with antibiotics for treating neonatal sepsis or NEC. Three comparisons were evaluated: (1) PTX with antibiotics versus placebo or no intervention with antibiotics, (2) PTX with antibiotics versus PTX with antibiotics and adjunct treatments like IgM-enriched intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG), and (3) PTX with antibiotics versus IgM-enriched IVIG with antibiotics. The analysis included six RCTs involving 416 neonates, all of whom had sepsis; no studies on neonates with NEC were identified. Four of the six trials were determined to have a high risk of bias in at least one domain. Comparison 1: PTX with antibiotics versus placebo or no intervention with antibiotics in neonates with sepsis. PTX may reduce all-cause mortality during the hospital stay (risk ratio [RR] 0.57, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.35 to 0.93; risk difference [RD] −0.08, 95% CI −0.14 to −0.01; number needed to treat for an additional beneficial outcome [NNTB] 13, 95% CI 7 to 100; 6 studies, 416 participants, low-certainty evidence). PTX may also decrease the length of hospital stay (mean difference [MD] −7.74 days, 95% CI −11.72 to −3.76; 2 studies, 157 participants, low-certainty evidence). The evidence is very uncertain regarding the effects of PTX on chronic lung disease (CLD) (RR 1.50, 95% CI 0.45 to 5.05; 1 study, 120 participants, very low-certainty evidence), severe intraventricular haemorrhage (sIVH) (RR 0.75, 95% CI 0.28 to 2.03; 1 study, 120 participants, very low-certainty evidence), periventricular leukomalacia (PVL) (RR 0.50, 95% CI 0.10 to 2.63; 1 study, 120 participants, very low-certainty evidence), NEC (RR 0.56, 95% CI 0.29 to 1.06; 6 studies, 405 participants, very low-certainty evidence), or retinopathy of prematurity (ROP) (RR 0.40, 95% CI 0.08 to 1.98; 1 study, 120 participants, very low-certainty evidence). Comparison 2: PTX with antibiotics versus PTX with antibiotics and IgM-enriched IVIG in neonates with sepsis. The evidence is very uncertain regarding the effect of PTX with antibiotics compared to PTX with antibiotics and IgM-enriched IVIG on mortality (RR 0.71, 95% CI 0.24 to 2.10; 1 study, 102 participants, very low-certainty evidence) or the development of NEC (RR 1.33, 95% CI 0.31 to 5.66; 1 study, 102 participants, very low-certainty evidence). Outcomes such as CLD, sIVH, PVL, length of hospital stay, and ROP were not reported in this comparison. Comparison 3: PTX with antibiotics versus IgM-enriched IVIG with antibiotics in neonates with sepsis. The evidence is very uncertain regarding the effect of PTX with antibiotics compared to IgM-enriched IVIG with antibiotics on mortality (RR 1.25, 95% CI 0.36 to 4.39; 1 study, 102 participants, very low-certainty evidence) or the development of NEC (RR 1.33, 95% CI 0.31 to 5.66; 1 study, 102 participants, very low-certainty evidence). Outcomes such as CLD, sIVH, PVL, length of hospital stay, and ROP were not reported in this comparison. Adverse effects of PTX were evaluated in all included studies, but no adverse effects were reported in the intervention group across any of the comparisons. Conclusions: Low-certainty evidence suggests that PTX, when used as an adjunct to antibiotics in neonatal sepsis, may reduce mortality and the length of hospital stay without causing adverse effects. However, the evidence is very uncertain regarding the comparative effects of PTX with antibiotics versus PTX with antibiotics and IgM-enriched IVIG, or PTX with antibiotics versus IgM-enriched IVIG with antibiotics, on mortality or the development of NEC. Further well-designed multicentre trials are needed to confirm or refute the effectiveness and safety of PTX in reducing mortality and morbidity in neonates with sepsis or NEC.
